spec.title: Sink rows per second (whole group)
spec.description: Rows the whole group inserts per second (sum over all consumers). Look for the step height when the consumers start and for how long it holds. Surprising: a plateau that does not change when more consumers or more partitions are added (then something else is the limit, see rows 2 and 3). Read it against runs.tsv: each run is one drain, the line falls to 0 when the topic is empty.

spec.title: Rows per second per consumer
spec.description: One line per consumer process (label instance = its metrics port, 8001 = consumer 1). Look for how many lines are above zero. Consumers that are alive but owned no partition show a flat line at 0. Surprising: lines of very different height with equal partition counts per consumer.

spec.title: Lag per partition
spec.description: Log end offset minus committed offset of the group, one line per partition (polled every 1 s by the consumers, the same value on every member, so max by partition). Look for lines falling together (every partition has an owner) or some staying flat (no owner yet) and for the last partitions finishing later (uneven split). Stale lines of the previous run can linger for a few minutes after a run ends.

spec.title: Total lag
spec.description: Sum of the lag over all partitions (rows still to read). It starts at the backlog (about 300,000) and should reach 0 at the end of each run. Surprising: it does not start at the same value in two runs of the same partition count.

spec.title: Assigned partitions per consumer
spec.description: ep_consumer_assigned_partitions per consumer process. This is the direct answer to which consumers have assignments: with P partitions and N consumers each owns about P/N, and with N > P the extra ones sit at 0. Surprising: the total of all lines is not P while the group is stable.

spec.title: Consumers with and without assignments
spec.description: Alive consumers (up = 1) split by whether they own at least one partition. The idle line is the extra-consumers effect. Surprising: idle consumers while N is lower than P.

spec.title: Rebalances (assignments received) per consumer
spec.description: increase() of ep_consumer_rebalances_total over the window. Each join of a consumer causes a rebalance for the whole group (eager round-robin assignor stops every member). Look for the burst at the start of every run. Surprising: rebalances while the drain is running (a consumer died or was too slow to heartbeat).

spec.title: Batch size (messages per fetched batch)
spec.description: Average messages handed to one eachBatch call (kind=batch). It can be at most CONSUMER_MAX_BATCH_SIZE (1000). Small batches mean the partition has little data buffered per fetch.

spec.title: Chunk processing time p50 / p99
spec.description: Whole chunk: parse, write, DLQ and offset commit (ep_consumer_batch_processing_seconds). In the delay sweep it includes SINK_PROCESSING_DELAY_MS. Look for p99 rising when more consumers are added: a shared limit (Postgres).

spec.title: Database write time p50 / p99
spec.description: One BEGIN..COMMIT of an insert chunk (ep_consumer_db_write_seconds). If this rises with the number of consumers, Postgres is the shared limit, not the partitions.

spec.title: Consumer cores busy (shared CPUs)
spec.description: Busy share (1 - idle) of each logical CPU the consumers are pinned to (variable cpu_consumers = 0,6,3,9,4,10; all consumers share these). These CPUs are also the broker CPUs in the drain part. Look for values near 1: then the consumers compete for CPU and the partition effect is mixed with a CPU limit.

spec.title: Postgres cores busy
spec.description: Busy share of the CPUs Postgres is pinned to (cpu_postgres = 1,7,2,8; the container has a quota of 2 CPUs, so at most about 2 cores of work). Look for it flat at its limit while the rows per second stops growing: the database is the bottleneck.

spec.title: Node process CPU per consumer
spec.description: user + system CPU seconds per second of each consumer process (1.0 = one full core). A single Node consumer is one thread: values near 1.0 mean that consumer is CPU-bound.

spec.title: Broker cores busy
spec.description: Busy share of the broker CPUs (cpu_kafka = 3,9,4,10, the same CPUs as the consumers in the drain part). The brokers only serve fetches in the drain, so I expect them to stay low.

spec.title: Postgres connections open
spec.description: Sum of ep_pg_pool_total over all consumers (each has a pool of up to 5, but one partition at a time uses one connection). Postgres max_connections is 100; with 12 consumers I do not expect to get near it.

spec.title: Duplicates and DLQ rows per second
spec.description: Rows absorbed by ON CONFLICT and records sent to the DLQ. Both must be 0 in every run (the table is cleaned before each drain, all records are valid). Anything above 0 invalidates the run.

spec.title: Failed chunks, commit errors, paused partitions
spec.description: Chunk attempts that failed and are retried, failed offset commits, and partitions paused because the DB is unavailable. All must be 0.

spec.title: Event loop lag p99 per consumer
spec.description: Main-thread delay of each consumer (nodejs_eventloop_lag_p99_seconds). Values above about 50 ms mean that consumer is CPU-saturated, which then limits the result.

spec.title: Scrape targets up
spec.description: Consumers Prometheus can scrape (up per instance, 12 targets are configured, the ones not running show 0 or nothing). Surprising: fewer up than consumers started: the group is not what the run thinks it is.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: how fast is the group, and what is left
2. The mechanism: who owns which partition
3. Resource view: where the cost lands
4. Validity checks: can I trust the run

spec.description: CPU ids the consumers group is pinned to (0,6,3,9,4,10), as a regex for cpu=~"$cpu_consumers"

spec.name: cpu_postgres
spec.label: CPUs: postgres (pinned)
spec.description: CPU ids the postgres group is pinned to (1,7,2,8), as a regex for cpu=~"$cpu_postgres"

spec.description: CPU ids the kafka group is pinned to (3,9,4,10), as a regex for cpu=~"$cpu_kafka"
